young.html: Have you ever said the wrong word by mistake, like calling your teacher "Mom"? Sigmund Freud, a doctor in Vienna, thought little mistakes like that were interesting. He wondered whether they showed something we were thinking about without noticing.

Later in his life Freud drew a picture of the mind as three parts that often argue. One part just wants things right now. One part is like a strict rule-keeper inside us. And one part, the "I", has to find a sensible way between them and the real world.

young.name: gb-freud-mind
young.cap: Choose a situation and hear the three "voices" of Freud's picture (our own examples). It is a picture, not something scientists have found in the brain.

young.html: Many people today find this picture a useful way to talk about feelings. Scientists also point out that it is hard to test, and they study the mind in other ways too.

Three voices. Think of a small choice you made today, like whether to do chores before play. Write what the "I want it now" voice said, what the "rules" voice said, and what you actually decided. Was it a good middle way?

full.text: From dreams to a theory of the mind

full.html: After The Interpretation of Dreams Freud wrote for almost forty more years. Volume 54 of the set gathers many of these works, among them his lectures at Clark University in Massachusetts (1909), papers on repression and the unconscious (1915), the General Introduction to Psychoanalysis (lectures given in Vienna in 1915–17), Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), The Ego and the Id (1923), Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and the New Introductory Lectures (1933).
In 1938, after Nazi Germany took over Austria, Freud and his family fled to London, where he died the next year. His daughter Anna Freud carried on his work with children.
The General Introduction starts with ordinary mistakes: slips of the tongue, forgetting a name, losing things. Freud argues that many of them are not chance.

full.text: They are not accidents, but valid psychic acts. They have their meaning; they arise through the collaboration, or better, the mutual interference, of two different intentions.
full.author: Sigmund Freud
full.work: A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis, Lecture III
full.tr: anonymous, with a preface by G. Stanley Hall

full.html: From slips and dreams he moves to his central claim, which he knew many listeners would resist:

full.text: The first of these displeasing assertions of psychoanalysis is this, that the psychic processes are in themselves unconscious, and that those which are conscious are merely isolated acts and parts of the total psychic life.
full.author: Sigmund Freud
full.work: A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis, Lecture I
full.tr: anonymous, with a preface by G. Stanley Hall

full.html: Later in the lectures he names three blows to human pride: Copernicus showed the earth is not the center of the universe; Darwin showed our descent from other animals; and psychology, he says, now shows the mind is not in charge of itself.

full.text: But the third and most irritating insult is flung at the human mania of greatness by present-day psychological research, which wants to prove to the "I" that it is not even master in its own home.
full.author: Sigmund Freud
full.work: A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis, Lecture XVIII
full.tr: anonymous, with a preface by G. Stanley Hall

full.html: In The Ego and the Id (1923) Freud gave his best-known model. In German he used plain words: das Es ("the It"), das Ich ("the I") and das Über-Ich ("the Over-I"). His English translators made them Latin: id, ego and superego.

head: Part
Freud's idea (our summary)
rows: Inborn drives that want satisfaction now, without regard to reality or rules.
The organizing self that deals with the real world and must find a way between the id's demands and the superego's.
The inner judge, formed from the rules and ideals of parents and society; the source of guilt.

full.name: gb-freud-mind
full.cap: Freud's three parts of the mind, in everyday situations (our examples).

full.html: Freud also described defenses, ways the ego protects itself from painful thoughts, such as repression (pushing a thought out of awareness). His daughter Anna Freud listed and described many more in 1936.

In Civilization and Its Discontents Freud asks why people are often unhappy in the very civilization that protects them. His answer: living together requires us to hold back strong drives, including aggression, and the superego turns that held-back force inward as guilt. Civilization, he thought, is worth its price, but the price is real.

full.text: How later research and critics judged him

full.html: Freud is one of the most influential thinkers of the 20th century, and one of the most argued about. His talking cure is the ancestor of many kinds of psychotherapy, and ideas such as defenses, the unconscious and the importance of childhood entered medicine, literature and daily speech. Critics raise serious objections: Freud built his theory mostly from his own patients and self-analysis, without controlled studies; the philosopher Karl Popper argued the theory could explain any outcome and so could not be tested; the philosopher Adolf Grünbaum (1984) and others questioned whether his case evidence showed what he claimed; and historians have found that some case reports were less successful than he said. On the other side, experimental psychology has confirmed in its own terms that much mental work happens outside awareness, and controlled trials of modern psychodynamic therapy, which grew from Freud's, have found benefits for some problems. Most psychologists today regard the id, ego and superego as a historical model rather than a scientific finding.
Thinking "unconscious" in Freud just means "asleep" or "knocked out." He meant thoughts and wishes active in the mind that a person is not aware of.

items: Plato's Republic divides the soul into three parts too: reason, spirit and appetite, with reason meant to rule. Compare Freud's ego, superego and id, and notice the differences.
Hobbes and Rousseau, earlier on this ladder, also asked what people give up to live in society; Freud's answer is psychological rather than political.
Nietzsche wrote before Freud about drives and the bad conscience; Freud said he avoided reading Nietzsche closely so as to keep his own ideas independent.
Writers on the 20th-century literature rungs, such as Woolf and Joyce, explored inner life and memory in a world that was reading Freud.
How much of what we do is decided by thoughts we do not notice?
Is guilt a useful guide, a burden, or both?
Can an idea be valuable for thinking even if it fails as science?
What does a person give up to live with others, and what do they gain?

questions: Have you ever made a slip of the tongue? Do you think it meant anything?
When you face a choice, do you ever feel two "voices" inside? What do they say?
Where do our ideas of right and wrong come from: family, friends, faith, books, or our own thinking?
Why do you think Freud called his three ideas "blows" to human pride?
What kind of evidence would you want before believing a theory about the mind?
care: Freud wrote for adults, and some of his theories concern adult matters. This rung presents his main ideas, his history and how critics and later research judged him, at a general level and with nothing explicit.
